analysis.one_liner: Phases out routine antibiotic use in livestock unless makers prove it safe for people.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee and its health subcommittee on March 14, 2011, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the FDA to deny new approvals for animal antibiotics also used in human medicine unless the manufacturer proves the nontherapeutic use (growth promotion, routine disease prevention) poses no risk of breeding antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Existing approvals for such uses would be withdrawn two years after passage unless the same safety showing was made. The point is to keep antibiotics working when people get sick.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on antibiotics to treat pneumonia, food poisoning, skin infections, and other common illnesses. The bill's own findings cite estimates that antibiotic-resistant infections cost Americans $16.6 to $26 billion a year in health care costs, and that 80% of antibacterial drugs sold in the U.S. in 2009 went to food animals rather than human medicine. It would also protect sick livestock from resistant bacteria by keeping drugs effective for genuine veterinary treatment.

how_it_helps.text: Defines 'critical antimicrobial animal drugs' as penicillins, tetracyclines, macrolides, and other drug classes used in human medicine, and bars FDA approval of nontherapeutic livestock uses unless the maker demonstrates a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from antimicrobial resistance.

Requires withdrawal of existing approvals for those nontherapeutic uses two years after enactment unless the same safety demonstration is made, with exemptions preserved for legitimate use to treat actual disease or prevent documented disease in a herd.

The bill's findings cite the FDA's own tally that 13.1 million kilograms of antibacterial drugs were sold for food animals in 2009 versus 3.3 million kilograms for human health — 80% of the total — and cite studies linking resistant Salmonella, Campylobacter, and E. coli in people to antibiotic use in animals.

It points to Denmark's similar ban, which regulators there testified produced a marked reduction in antimicrobial resistance, and notes backing from the American Medical Association and more than 300 health, consumer, and agricultural organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Animal drug manufacturers selling antibiotics for growth promotion and routine feeding, and large-scale livestock producers — swine, cattle, and poultry operations — that rely on routine dosing to fatten animals cheaply and compensate for crowded conditions. Those costs could be passed to consumers through slightly higher meat prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Animal drug makers and big livestock producers

drawbacks.text: Livestock producers argue routine antibiotics lower production costs and keep meat affordable, and that a phaseout could raise feed and management costs, with some of that passed to consumers at the grocery store.

The bill's own findings acknowledge federal agencies do not collect the data on antibiotic use in animals needed to assess human health risks, so implementation would require building a regulatory record largely from scratch, and a two-year withdrawal timeline would be a sharp adjustment for producers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit — keeping antibiotics effective against serious infections — is long-term and broad, and the Danish experience suggests resistance falls when routine agricultural dosing stops. The costs fall on a specific industry: producers using cheap routine antibiotics to gain weight and prevent disease in crowded herds, and the companies that sell them those drugs. The tradeoff favors the public, though the two-year timeline and the lack of baseline usage data make the transition genuinely costly for some farms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Louise Slaughter introduced the bill on March 9, 2011.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Rules Committee, then on March 14 to the Energy and Commerce Health subcommittee.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in the record for the rest of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013.
The bill had 92 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Animal drug manufacturers and large livestock producers kept routine antibiotic feeding untouched, with no FDA review of the safety of nontherapeutic uses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Animal drug makers and industrial farms

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred; all 92 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would deny new approvals and withdraw existing ones for nontherapeutic livestock uses of medically important antibiotics unless safety from resistance is proven, eliminating a major market. Keeping antibiotics working for human medicine is the public's interest here.

Routine antibiotic feeding lowers their production costs, so a phaseout raises them, but the bill would preserve legitimate use to treat sick animals. The public interest is meat free of resistant bacteria and antibiotics that still work for people.
